162.title: Bereshit: two creation accounts (Genesis 1–2)
162.hook: chapter one is vast and ordered, chapter two close and earthy; tradition holds both
162.tomorrow: Bereshit: one person, a whole world
162.howItsDone: Jewish readers study Genesis 1 and 2 side by side in the portion of Bereshit, often with midrash on the two names of God and modern commentary on the two accounts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah's first letter, bet: closed behind, open ahead. Your line was open ahead.

Two photographs of the same person sit side by side. One is taken from a drone, high above a crowded square: a tiny figure, part of a vast pattern. The other is a close-up: the lines around the eyes, a smudge of flour on one cheek. Which one is true? Both. They just stand in different places. The first two chapters of Genesis are like that. Creation is told, then told again, and the two tellings don't sound alike.
screen: `A DRONE SHOT OF A CROWDED SQUARE.` → `A CLOSE-UP WITH FLOUR ON ONE CHEEK.` → `CREATION, TOLD TWICE.`

segments.voice: Chapter one is the drone shot. Vast and ordered: light, sky, sea and land, plants, lights in the sky, fish and birds, animals. Six days, each ending, and there was evening and there was morning. God speaks, and it is. Human beings come last, all at once: "male and female created He them," in the image of God. Chapter two is the close-up. Suddenly the story is on the ground. No plants yet, no rain; a mist waters the earth. God, now called by a different name, the LORD God, "formed man of the dust of the ground," and breathes into his nostrils the breath of life. In Hebrew the human is adam and the ground is adamah; the two words sound alike. Then a garden, a river, animals brought to be named, and a partner built from his side. Two tellings, two orders, even two names of God. People read this in different ways. Some modern scholars say two older sources were woven together. Traditional commentators read one Torah showing two sides of the same truth. The midrash notices the two names: one stands for God's justice, the other for God's mercy, and the world was made with both, because it couldn't stand on either alone. A modern teacher, Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik, wrote of two Adams: one who builds and masters the world, and one who is lonely and longs for a companion and for God. Every person, he said, is both. Read this way, the Torah doesn't choose between the drone and the close-up. It keeps both photographs, side by side.
screen: `CHAPTER ONE: VAST AND ORDERED.` · `CHAPTER TWO: DUST AND BREATH.` · `JUSTICE AND MERCY, TWO NAMES.` · `TWO ADAMS IN EVERY PERSON.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: First, the drone shot: see yourself from high above, one small person in a huge, ordered world, and stay there a few breaths. Then come down close: your breath in your nostrils, your hands, the dust and warmth of you. Don't choose; let both be true at once.
Bereshit. The first portion, where creation is told twice, vast and close, and the tradition keeps both.
Your line: both are true. Two photographs, one person, and neither one is wrong. See you tomorrow.

163.title: Bereshit: one person, a whole world
163.hook: one human was created first, the Mishnah says, to teach that one life is a whole world (Sanhedrin 4:5)
163.tomorrow: Bereshit: you can rule over it
163.howItsDone: Jews often quote Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, that saving one life is like saving a whole world, when teaching about human dignity, medicine and the value of every person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation told twice: the drone shot and the close-up. Your line was both are true.

A courtroom, as the Mishnah describes it. A life is at stake: the charge carries the death penalty. Before the witnesses speak, the judges take them aside. They don't just say, tell the truth. They make them sit through a short lesson from the book of Genesis, about why God began the human race with just one person. Today, the lesson those witnesses heard.
screen: `A COURTROOM, A LIFE AT STAKE.` → `THE JUDGES TAKE THE WITNESSES ASIDE.` → `A LESSON FROM GENESIS FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's in the Mishnah, tractate Sanhedrin. Why was the first human created alone? The Mishnah gives several answers. First: whoever destroys a single life, scripture counts it as if they destroyed a whole world. And whoever sustains a single life, as if they sustained a whole world. Adam was one person, and from him came everyone, so every single person carries a whole world inside. Second: for the sake of peace. Since everyone comes from one ancestor, no one can say, my father is greater than yours. Third: to show God's greatness. When a person stamps coins from one mold, the Mishnah says, they all come out alike. But God stamped every human from the mold of the first, and not one is like another. Then the Mishnah draws a startling conclusion. Each person is obligated to say: for my sake the world was created. Later teachers read that not as arrogance but as responsibility: if the world was made for you, you're answerable for it. And if it was made for them too, every person you meet is a whole world. That's what the witnesses were meant to feel. You're not testifying about a case. You're holding a world in your hands.
screen: `ONE LIFE IS A WHOLE WORLD.` · `NO ONE CAN SAY MY FATHER IS GREATER.` · `ONE MOLD, AND NO TWO ALIKE.` · `FOR MY SAKE THE WORLD WAS CREATED.` · then, large: `EACH LIFE A WORLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today, maybe someone you usually barely notice: a cashier, a neighbor, a coworker. Picture everything inside them: their childhood, the people they love, what they're afraid of, what they hope for this year. Stay a minute with that world, as full as yours.
Bereshit. The first portion, where one human is created first, to teach that each life is a whole world.
Your line: each life a world. Every one of them, yours included. That's day one hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 163 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BERESHIT: YOU CAN RULE OVER IT.`

164.title: Bereshit: you can rule over it (Genesis 4:7)
164.hook: God tells Cain the urge crouches, but he can master it
164.howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching speaks of the yetzer hara and the yetzer hatov, the selfish and the good inclinations, and treats study, prayer and habit as ways to steer the urge rather than erase it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's lesson: one person created first, because each life is a whole world. Your line was each life a world.

You know the moment. Someone says something sharp, and a reply rises in your throat, already loaded. The phone is face-down on the table and your hand is already reaching. A terrible day, and the cabinet with the cookies right there. The pull feels like it's already decided. Cain knew that moment. His offering wasn't accepted and his brother's was, his face fell, and something hot rose in him. And right then, before anything happened, God spoke to him.
screen: `A REPLY RISES, ALREADY LOADED.` → `CAIN'S FACE FELL.` → `BEFORE ANYTHING HAPPENED, GOD SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it." Sin crouches at the door, like an animal waiting. It wants you. But you can rule over it. It's the first time the word sin appears in the Torah, and it arrives with a promise: you're not helpless. The rabbis gave that crouching thing a name: yetzer hara, the evil inclination, or better, the selfish urge. Yetzer comes from a root meaning to form, the same root used when God formed the first human from the dust. The urge is part of how people are made. And here's the surprise: the rabbis don't call it simply bad. The midrash says that without it, no one would build a house, marry, have children or start a business. That's why, it says, God looked at creation and called it very good, urge and all. The urge is energy; the question is who's steering. The Talmud has God say: I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its remedy. And Pirkei Avot asks: who is mighty? The one who conquers their own urge, not the one who never feels it. Cain, the story goes on, didn't rule it. He went out to the field with his brother. But the verse was spoken before that, and it stayed in the Torah for everyone after him. The urge crouches. It isn't the one in charge. You can rule it.
screen: `SIN CROUCHES AT THE DOOR.` · `YETZER: FROM THE ROOT TO FORM.` · `WITHOUT IT, NO ONE BUILDS A HOUSE.` · `WHO IS MIGHTY? WHO RULES THE URGE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN RULE IT.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and within a minute some urge will show up: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, check the time, open your eyes. Don't fight it and don't follow it; just notice it crouching at the door, and name it: there's the urge. Breathe once more before you do anything, because that breath is ruling it.
Yetzer hara. The selfish urge: part of how we're formed, full of energy, crouching at the door, and something a person can rule.
Your line: you can rule it. The urge is energy, and you do the steering. Day one hundred sixty-four in the books.

165.title: Bereshit: walking with God (Genesis 5:24)
165.hook: among long lists of generations, Enoch "walked with God, and he was not"
165.howItsDone: Jewish readers study the genealogies of Genesis 5 with Rashi and the midrash, and 'walking with God' is often taught as a picture of a steady, everyday religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yetzer hara, the urge that crouches at the door. Your line was you can rule it.

Some families keep a list like this: a page in the front of an old Bible, a spreadsheet a cousin made, a chart on a genealogy site. Names, dates, who begat whom. Most of it gets skimmed. Genesis chapter five is that list, from Adam to Noah. Each man is born, has a son, lives so many years, has other sons and daughters. And then, again and again, the same closing words: and he died. And he died. And he died. Like a drumbeat. Until one name, where the drumbeat breaks.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES YOU SKIM.` → `AND HE DIED. AND HE DIED.` → `ONE NAME BREAKS THE DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: His name is Enoch, seventh from Adam. Instead of and he died, the Torah says: "And Enoch walked with God, and he was not; for God took him." One verse, and he's gone. The Torah doesn't explain it. What does he was not mean? The rabbis disagree. The midrash records a debate: some teachers read it as praise, others as something more complicated. Rashi says Enoch was righteous, but easily swayed, so God took him early, before he could go wrong. Enoch lived three hundred sixty-five years, far fewer than the others on the list. Other ancient Jewish writings, outside the Hebrew Bible, told great stories of Enoch rising to heaven. The Torah itself says only this. Now the verb, walked. In Hebrew it's vayithalech, a form that can mean walked about, kept walking. Some readers hear in it a way of life, not a single trip: going through the days with God alongside. The phrase comes back soon, about another man; you'll hear it tomorrow. And that's the first portion, Bereshit, finished. A letter open ahead. Creation told twice. One person, a whole world. An urge you can rule. And, in a long list of names, one man who walked with God. The portion ends on a quiet line: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." A door, open ahead, into the next portion.
screen: `AND HE DIED. AND HE DIED.` · `ENOCH WALKED WITH GOD, AND WAS NOT.` · `THE RABBIS DISAGREE WHY.` · `WALKED: A WAY OF LIFE.` · then, large: `WALK WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Imagine walking at an easy pace down a quiet road, one step with each breath in, one with each breath out. If you pray, picture God walking beside you; if you don't, picture whatever you most want beside you on the road: goodness, patience, someone you love. Don't hurry; just keep walking.
Bereshit. The first portion: from the first letter to Enoch, who walked with God, to Noah, who found grace.
Your line: walk with God. That's one whole portion finished, and day one hundred sixty-five.

166.title: Noach: whole-hearted (Genesis 6:9)
166.hook: the portion opens by calling Noah tamim, whole
166.howItsDone: Parashat Noach, Genesis 6:9–11:32, is read on the second Shabbat after Simchat Torah; teachers often begin with the debate over 'in his generations' in Rashi and the Talmud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Enoch, who walked with God, and the end of the first portion. Your line was walk with God.

Lunch eaten while answering email. A friend heard while half-reading a text. A show watched while scrolling another screen. A lot of life gets done with part of you, and the rest somewhere else. And then there are moments done with all of a person: holding a newborn, playing music, a conversation so good the time disappears. The second portion of the Torah describes its hero with a Hebrew word for exactly that.
screen: `LUNCH, EMAIL, ANOTHER SCREEN.` → `A MOMENT WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD FOR A WHOLE PERSON.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Noach, Noah, and it begins: "These are the generations of Noah. Noah was in his generations a man righteous and whole-hearted; Noah walked with God." There's yesterday's phrase again: walked with God. And there's today's word. Whole-hearted, in Hebrew, is tamim: whole, complete, without a crack. The same word describes an animal fit for an offering: unblemished, nothing missing. Later, God tells Abraham, walk before me and be tamim. And Moses tells the people, "Thou shalt be whole-hearted with the LORD thy God." It's not a word for perfect, as in never making mistakes. It's a word for undivided: all of you, in one place. Then the rabbis notice two small words: in his generations. Why add that? The Talmud records a disagreement. One teacher says it's praise: if Noah was righteous even in a violent generation, imagine him in a good one. Another says it's a limit: righteous for his generation; in Abraham's time, he wouldn't have stood out. Rashi quotes both, and doesn't choose. Either way, the text sets Noah's wholeness in a world coming apart. The verses right after say the earth was filled with violence. In the middle of that, one person was undivided. That's what tamim asks. Not perfection. Wholeness, in whatever generation you're in.
screen: `NOAH WAS RIGHTEOUS AND WHOLE-HEARTED.` · `TAMIM: WHOLE, WITHOUT A CRACK.` · `NOT PERFECT. UNDIVIDED.` · `IN HIS GENERATIONS: PRAISE OR LIMIT?` · then, large: `WHOLE-HEARTED.`

segments.voice: Notice where the parts of you are: some in this room, some in a worry about tomorrow, some in a conversation from yesterday. Call each part back, one at a time, like calling people to the table, and be here, all of you, for one breath, then another. If a part wanders off, call it back without scolding.
Tamim. Whole, complete, undivided: the word the Torah uses for Noah, and for being whole-hearted with God.
Your line: whole-hearted. All of you, gathered in one place. See you on the ark, tomorrow.

167.title: Noach: the window (Genesis 6:16)
167.hook: the ark had a tzohar for light; midrash says it was a glowing stone
167.howItsDone: Jewish readers study the tzohar with Rashi and the midrash, and Hasidic teachers use the double meaning of teivah, ark and word, to teach about entering the words of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tamim: Noah was whole-hearted, undivided, in a world coming apart. Your line was whole-hearted.

Forget the picture-book ark with a giraffe's head poking out the top. The Torah's ark is a huge wooden box, sealed with pitch inside and out, three decks, crowded with animals and Noah's family. The rain falls for forty days. The door is shut; the text says God shut it. Then the waiting, month after month as the text counts them, inside. How does anyone live in a closed box that long? The blueprint God gives Noah is only a few verses. But one line in it is about light.
screen: `A HUGE SEALED WOODEN BOX.` → `THE DOOR IS SHUT, MONTH AFTER MONTH.` → `ONE LINE ABOUT LIGHT.`

segments.voice: God tells Noah to make a tzohar for the ark, and finish it a cubit from the top. What's a tzohar? It's a rare word, and nobody is completely sure. Some readers hear in it tzohorayim, noon, the brightest part of the day, so something to do with light. The rabbis in the midrash offer two answers, and Rashi repeats both. One teacher says it was a window, an opening near the roof. Another says it was a precious stone, a gem that glowed and lit the ark from within. A window lets light in from outside. A glowing stone makes light inside, even when outside is dark. The window says: even in a flood, keep one opening to the world; don't seal yourself in completely. The stone says: when there's no light outside at all, carry some within. Much later, Hasidic teachers played with a different word in the same verse. The Hebrew for ark, teivah, also means a word. So when God tells Noah to come into the teivah, they heard: come into the word. Step inside the words of your prayer, or your study, and make them a shelter with a light in them. And some readers notice what the plan leaves out: no rudder, no oars, no sail. Noah, as the text tells it, doesn't steer. What he could do was make sure there was light inside.
screen: `TZOHAR: A RARE WORD FOR LIGHT.` · `A WINDOW, OR A GLOWING STONE.` · `TEIVAH: AN ARK, AND A WORD.` · `NO RUDDER, BUT LIGHT INSIDE.` · then, large: `MAKE A WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Think of something that feels like a flood right now, a worry, a hard stretch. Find one window, one person or place that opens onto the world outside it, and then one stone, a small light you carry inside: a memory, a word, a reason. Rest your attention on that light, and let it glow.
Tzohar. The ark's source of light, a rare word: a window, some say, and some say a glowing stone.
Your line: make a window. A window or a stone, and either way, light. That's one hundred sixty-seven days.

168.title: Noach: laws for everyone (Genesis 9:1–7)
168.hook: the rabbis drew seven laws for all humanity from Noah's covenant
168.howItsDone: Jewish law teaches seven Noahide laws as the basic obligations God asks of all humanity, and, following Rabbi Joshua in the Tosefta, holds that the righteous of every nation have a share in the world to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tzohar: a window, or a glowing stone, light inside the ark. Your line was make a window.

The ark has landed. The ground is drying. Noah and his family step out onto an empty earth, the animals scattering into the hills. Everyone alive on the planet is in this one small group. Whatever comes next, every nation, every language, every person who will ever live, starts here. So what does God say to them first? Not a law for one people. A covenant with all of them, and through them with everyone.
screen: `THE ARK HAS LANDED.` → `EVERYONE ALIVE, IN ONE GROUP.` → `A COVENANT WITH ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: God blesses Noah and his sons: be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth. The animals are given as food, but with a limit: don't eat flesh with its life, its blood, still in it. Then the heart of it: "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God made He man." The verse grounds the worth of every human life in God's image. A few verses later comes the rainbow, the sign that the flood will never come again. From these verses, and a few others, the rabbis of the Talmud drew seven basic laws for all humanity, called the laws of the children of Noah. Six are things not to do: no idolatry, no cursing God, no murder, no sexual immorality, no theft, and no eating a limb torn from a living animal. One is something to do: set up courts of justice. Every person on earth, in this view, is a child of Noah, and these are the basic decencies God asks of everyone. In this tradition, the Torah's commandments as a whole are for Jews; for everyone else, these seven. And in the Tosefta, Rabbi Joshua teaches that the righteous of the nations have a share in the world to come. So, in this view, no one needs to become Jewish to be righteous. The seven laws are a Jewish framework, drawn from a Jewish reading of the text. But look at most of the list: don't kill, don't steal, don't be cruel to animals, have courts. Much of it reads like a floor of basic decency.
screen: `FOR IN THE IMAGE OF GOD MADE HE MAN.` · `SEVEN LAWS FOR THE CHILDREN OF NOAH.` · `SIX DON'TS AND ONE DO: COURTS.` · `THE RIGHTEOUS OF ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `LAWS FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Think of the most different person you can imagine: far away, another language, another faith, another life. Ask what you share, not beliefs but basic decencies: don't take a life, don't take what isn't yours, be fair, be kind to animals. Let each one come slowly, and picture that person keeping them too.
